items.title: I can define an inertial reference frame and give examples
items.what: An inertial reference frame is one that is either stationary or moving at a constant velocity — it is not accelerating. Any frame moving at constant velocity relative to another inertial frame is also inertial.
items.why: Special relativity only applies to inertial frames. Identifying whether a frame is inertial or not is the first step in solving any relativity problem.
items.example: A train carriage moving at a steady 100 km/h on a straight track is an inertial frame. The same carriage while braking is a non-inertial frame because it is accelerating.

subtopic.name: Foundations of Special Relativity
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces inertial reference frames, Einstein's two postulates, and the Michelson–Morley experiment. It explains why classical (Newtonian) mechanics breaks down at speeds approaching the speed of light.
subtopic.why: Understanding the foundations gives students the conceptual basis for all the mathematical consequences of special relativity. Without a clear grasp of what a reference frame is and why the speed of light is constant, the equations for time dilation and length contraction have no meaning.

items.title: I can identify whether a given reference frame is inertial or non-inertial
items.what: A reference frame is non-inertial if it is accelerating — including speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction. A satellite in circular orbit is technically non-inertial because its direction is always changing.
items.why: Correct identification of frame type is needed before applying the postulates or equations of special relativity.
items.example: A rocket travelling at a constant 0.5c in a straight line is inertial. A rocket that is firing its engines and speeding up is non-inertial.

subtopic.name: Foundations of Special Relativity
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces inertial reference frames, Einstein's two postulates, and the Michelson–Morley experiment. It explains why classical (Newtonian) mechanics breaks down at speeds approaching the speed of light.
subtopic.why: Understanding the foundations gives students the conceptual basis for all the mathematical consequences of special relativity. Without a clear grasp of what a reference frame is and why the speed of light is constant, the equations for time dilation and length contraction have no meaning.

items.title: I can state Einstein's first postulate: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames
items.what: No inertial reference frame is special or preferred. Any experiment performed in one inertial frame will give the same result as the same experiment performed in any other inertial frame.
items.why: This postulate means that there is no absolute rest frame — you cannot perform an experiment inside a smoothly moving vehicle to determine whether you are moving or stationary.
items.example: A person on a smoothly moving train dropping a ball sees it fall straight down, just as someone standing on a platform would see a ball fall straight down. The physics is the same in both frames.

subtopic.name: Foundations of Special Relativity
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces inertial reference frames, Einstein's two postulates, and the Michelson–Morley experiment. It explains why classical (Newtonian) mechanics breaks down at speeds approaching the speed of light.
subtopic.why: Understanding the foundations gives students the conceptual basis for all the mathematical consequences of special relativity. Without a clear grasp of what a reference frame is and why the speed of light is constant, the equations for time dilation and length contraction have no meaning.

items.title: I can state Einstein's second postulate: the speed of light is constant for all observers
items.what: The speed of light in a vacuum, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, is the same for all observers regardless of the motion of the observer or the source of the light.
items.why: This postulate directly contradicts classical physics, where velocities add together. It is the reason time dilation and length contraction must occur — space and time must adjust so that every observer always measures light at c.
items.example: A rocket moving away from Earth at 0.5c turns on its headlights. An observer on Earth and the rocket crew both measure the light from those headlights travelling at exactly c, not at 1.5c or 0.5c.

subtopic.name: Foundations of Special Relativity
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces inertial reference frames, Einstein's two postulates, and the Michelson–Morley experiment. It explains why classical (Newtonian) mechanics breaks down at speeds approaching the speed of light.
subtopic.why: Understanding the foundations gives students the conceptual basis for all the mathematical consequences of special relativity. Without a clear grasp of what a reference frame is and why the speed of light is constant, the equations for time dilation and length contraction have no meaning.

items.title: I can explain why the null result of the Michelson–Morley experiment supports Einstein's theory
items.what: The Michelson–Morley experiment attempted to detect the luminiferous aether — a medium thought to carry light — by measuring changes in the speed of light in different directions relative to Earth's motion. The experiment found no difference at all (the null result).
items.why: The null result showed that light does not require a medium to travel through and that its speed is the same in all directions. This was direct evidence that the speed of light is constant for all observers, consistent with Einstein's second postulate.
items.example: If the aether existed, the two beams of light in the interferometer would return at different times (like a swimmer going with and against a current). But both beams always returned together, indicating the speed of light was the same in all directions.

subtopic.name: Foundations of Special Relativity
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces inertial reference frames, Einstein's two postulates, and the Michelson–Morley experiment. It explains why classical (Newtonian) mechanics breaks down at speeds approaching the speed of light.
subtopic.why: Understanding the foundations gives students the conceptual basis for all the mathematical consequences of special relativity. Without a clear grasp of what a reference frame is and why the speed of light is constant, the equations for time dilation and length contraction have no meaning.

items.title: I can compare Einstein's special relativity with the predictions of classical physics
items.what: Classical (Newtonian) physics assumes that velocities add directly and that time and length are absolute — the same for all observers. Special relativity replaces these assumptions: time and length are relative, and the speed of light is absolute.
items.why: Understanding this contrast shows where classical mechanics fails — at speeds approaching c — and why a new framework was needed.
items.example: Classical physics predicts that if a train moves at 0.5c and its headlights emit light, an observer on the ground measures that light at 1.5c. Special relativity says the observer measures it at c. Experiments confirm special relativity is correct.

subtopic.name: Foundations of Special Relativity
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces inertial reference frames, Einstein's two postulates, and the Michelson–Morley experiment. It explains why classical (Newtonian) mechanics breaks down at speeds approaching the speed of light.
subtopic.why: Understanding the foundations gives students the conceptual basis for all the mathematical consequences of special relativity. Without a clear grasp of what a reference frame is and why the speed of light is constant, the equations for time dilation and length contraction have no meaning.

items.title: I can define proper time (t₀) and identify which observer measures it
items.what: Proper time is the time interval between two events measured in the reference frame where both events occur at the same point in space. It is always the shortest time interval measured for those two events.
items.why: Correctly identifying who measures proper time is the critical first step in applying the time dilation formula. Applying the formula backwards gives an incorrect, physically impossible answer.
items.example: A clock on a rocket ticks twice. The rocket crew sees both ticks happen at the same location (the clock), so they measure proper time. An Earth observer sees the clock move between the two ticks, so they measure dilated time.

subtopic.name: Time Dilation
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the concept of proper time, dilated time, and the Lorentz factor. Students learn to identify which observer measures proper time and apply the equation t = γt₀ to calculate time intervals in different reference frames.
subtopic.why: Time dilation is one of the most experimentally verified predictions of special relativity, confirmed by atomic clocks on aircraft and by the observed lifetimes of fast-moving particles. It underpins GPS corrections and particle physics calculations.

items.title: I can define dilated time (t) and explain why it is longer than proper time
items.what: Dilated time is the time interval between two events measured by an observer in a frame where the two events occur at different points in space. It is always longer than the proper time for the same pair of events.
items.why: Because the speed of light is constant, an observer who sees the light clock move must observe the light travel a longer diagonal path — meaning more time must pass in their frame.
items.example: A rocket crew measures a light flash lasting 0.100 s (proper time). An Earth observer watching the rocket pass at 0.866c measures the same flash lasting 0.200 s — the dilated time.

subtopic.name: Time Dilation
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the concept of proper time, dilated time, and the Lorentz factor. Students learn to identify which observer measures proper time and apply the equation t = γt₀ to calculate time intervals in different reference frames.
subtopic.why: Time dilation is one of the most experimentally verified predictions of special relativity, confirmed by atomic clocks on aircraft and by the observed lifetimes of fast-moving particles. It underpins GPS corrections and particle physics calculations.

items.title: I can define and calculate the Lorentz factor (γ)
items.what: The Lorentz factor γ = 1 / √(1 − v²/c²) describes how much time, length, and energy differ between two reference frames. It is always greater than or equal to 1, and increases toward infinity as v approaches c.
items.why: The Lorentz factor appears in every relativistic equation. Being able to calculate it quickly and accurately is essential for all time dilation, length contraction, and energy calculations.

subtopic.name: Time Dilation
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the concept of proper time, dilated time, and the Lorentz factor. Students learn to identify which observer measures proper time and apply the equation t = γt₀ to calculate time intervals in different reference frames.
subtopic.why: Time dilation is one of the most experimentally verified predictions of special relativity, confirmed by atomic clocks on aircraft and by the observed lifetimes of fast-moving particles. It underpins GPS corrections and particle physics calculations.

items.title: I can apply the time dilation formula t = γt₀ to find dilated time or proper time
items.what: The equation t = γt₀ relates proper time t₀ (measured by the observer for whom the events occur at the same place) to dilated time t (measured by any other observer). Since γ ≥ 1, dilated time is always greater than or equal to proper time.
items.why: This formula is the primary mathematical tool for time dilation problems in VCE Physics. It is applied in contexts ranging from particle decay to GPS satellite corrections.
items.example: A muon at rest decays after t₀ = 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ s. Moving at 0.995c (γ = 10.01), an Earth observer measures t = 10.01 × 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ = 2.20 × 10⁻⁵ s.

subtopic.name: Time Dilation
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the concept of proper time, dilated time, and the Lorentz factor. Students learn to identify which observer measures proper time and apply the equation t = γt₀ to calculate time intervals in different reference frames.
subtopic.why: Time dilation is one of the most experimentally verified predictions of special relativity, confirmed by atomic clocks on aircraft and by the observed lifetimes of fast-moving particles. It underpins GPS corrections and particle physics calculations.

items.title: I can calculate the speed of an object given proper time and dilated time measurements
items.what: By rearranging t = γt₀ to find γ, and then rearranging γ = 1 / √(1 − v²/c²) to find v, it is possible to determine the relative speed between two frames from time measurements alone.
items.why: This reverse calculation is a common exam question style. It tests deep understanding of the relationship between γ and velocity, not just formula recall.
items.example: A particle is observed to decay after 45.2 ps when moving and 3.44 ps when at rest. γ = 45.2 / 3.44 = 13.14. Then v/c = √(1 − 1/13.14²) = 0.997, so v = 0.997c.

subtopic.name: Time Dilation
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the concept of proper time, dilated time, and the Lorentz factor. Students learn to identify which observer measures proper time and apply the equation t = γt₀ to calculate time intervals in different reference frames.
subtopic.why: Time dilation is one of the most experimentally verified predictions of special relativity, confirmed by atomic clocks on aircraft and by the observed lifetimes of fast-moving particles. It underpins GPS corrections and particle physics calculations.

items.title: I can explain what happens to dilated time as relative speed increases
items.what: As relative speed increases, the Lorentz factor γ increases. This means the difference between proper time and dilated time grows larger. As v approaches c, dilated time approaches infinity.
items.why: Understanding this trend qualitatively allows students to check whether calculated answers are physically reasonable and to explain graph-based questions about relativistic effects.
items.example: At v = 0.5c, γ ≈ 1.15, so a 1-second proper time becomes 1.15 s dilated. At v = 0.99c, γ ≈ 7.09, so the same 1-second proper time becomes 7.09 s dilated.

subtopic.name: Time Dilation
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the concept of proper time, dilated time, and the Lorentz factor. Students learn to identify which observer measures proper time and apply the equation t = γt₀ to calculate time intervals in different reference frames.
subtopic.why: Time dilation is one of the most experimentally verified predictions of special relativity, confirmed by atomic clocks on aircraft and by the observed lifetimes of fast-moving particles. It underpins GPS corrections and particle physics calculations.

items.title: I can define proper length (L₀) and identify which observer measures it
items.what: Proper length is the length of an object or distance measured by an observer who is at rest relative to the object or the two points defining the length. It is always the longest length measurement for that object.
items.why: Identifying who measures proper length is the critical first step for length contraction problems. Getting this wrong leads to an answer that is longer than the proper length, which is physically impossible.
items.example: A rocket crew measures the length of their own rocket to be 100 m. Since they are at rest relative to the rocket, this is the proper length. An Earth observer watching the rocket fly past measures a shorter, contracted length.

subtopic.name: Length Contraction
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers proper length, contracted length, and the application of L = L₀/γ. It examines which observer measures the proper length and how contraction only occurs in the direction of relative motion.
subtopic.why: Length contraction is the spatial counterpart of time dilation. Together they ensure that all observers measure the same speed of light. Length contraction also has direct engineering consequences — particle accelerator drift tubes must be designed with it in mind.

items.title: I can define contracted length (L) and explain why it is shorter than proper length
items.what: Contracted length is the length of a moving object or distance measured by an observer in relative motion with respect to that object. It is always less than the proper length for the same object.
items.why: Length contraction follows directly from the constancy of the speed of light and the definition of simultaneity. It is not an optical illusion — it is a real physical consequence of relative motion.
items.example: A platform is 500 m long as measured by a person standing on it (proper length). A rocket crew passing at 0.866c (γ = 2) measures the platform to be 500 / 2 = 250 m long.

subtopic.name: Length Contraction
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers proper length, contracted length, and the application of L = L₀/γ. It examines which observer measures the proper length and how contraction only occurs in the direction of relative motion.
subtopic.why: Length contraction is the spatial counterpart of time dilation. Together they ensure that all observers measure the same speed of light. Length contraction also has direct engineering consequences — particle accelerator drift tubes must be designed with it in mind.

items.title: I can apply the length contraction formula L = L₀/γ to various situations
items.what: The equation L = L₀/γ relates proper length L₀ to contracted length L. Since γ ≥ 1, contracted length is always ≤ proper length. Rearranging gives L₀ = Lγ, which is used when the contracted length is given and the proper length is unknown.
items.why: This formula is used directly in VCE exam questions involving rockets, platforms, particle accelerators, and muon travel distances.
items.example: A rocket of proper length 200 m passes Earth at 0.700c (γ = 1.40). The Earth observer measures its length as L = 200 / 1.40 = 143 m.

subtopic.name: Length Contraction
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers proper length, contracted length, and the application of L = L₀/γ. It examines which observer measures the proper length and how contraction only occurs in the direction of relative motion.
subtopic.why: Length contraction is the spatial counterpart of time dilation. Together they ensure that all observers measure the same speed of light. Length contraction also has direct engineering consequences — particle accelerator drift tubes must be designed with it in mind.

items.title: I can state that length contraction only occurs in the direction of relative motion
items.what: Special relativity predicts that an object contracts only along the axis parallel to its direction of travel relative to the observer. Dimensions perpendicular to the direction of motion are unchanged.
items.why: This is a common point of confusion. Students sometimes incorrectly apply length contraction to all dimensions of an object.
items.example: A square spacecraft 50 m × 50 m moving horizontally at 0.866c (γ = 2) is measured by an Earth observer to be 25 m long in the direction of travel but still 50 m wide.

subtopic.name: Length Contraction
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers proper length, contracted length, and the application of L = L₀/γ. It examines which observer measures the proper length and how contraction only occurs in the direction of relative motion.
subtopic.why: Length contraction is the spatial counterpart of time dilation. Together they ensure that all observers measure the same speed of light. Length contraction also has direct engineering consequences — particle accelerator drift tubes must be designed with it in mind.

items.title: I can calculate the speed of an object given its proper length and contracted length
items.what: By finding γ = L₀ / L from measured lengths, and then rearranging γ to solve for v, the relative speed between two frames can be determined from length measurements.
items.why: This tests the same algebraic reasoning as the reverse time dilation calculation and is a common exam question style.
items.example: A rocket's proper length is 60.0 m. An observer measures it as 14.0 m. γ = 60.0 / 14.0 = 4.286. Then v = c × √(1 − 1/4.286²) = 0.971c.

subtopic.name: Length Contraction
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers proper length, contracted length, and the application of L = L₀/γ. It examines which observer measures the proper length and how contraction only occurs in the direction of relative motion.
subtopic.why: Length contraction is the spatial counterpart of time dilation. Together they ensure that all observers measure the same speed of light. Length contraction also has direct engineering consequences — particle accelerator drift tubes must be designed with it in mind.

items.title: I can explain what happens to contracted length as relative speed increases
items.what: As relative speed increases, γ increases, so the contracted length decreases further. As v approaches c, the contracted length approaches zero.
items.why: This qualitative understanding is needed for graph-based questions and for checking whether calculated answers are physically reasonable.
items.example: At v = 0.5c (γ ≈ 1.15), a 100 m rocket appears 87 m long. At v = 0.99c (γ ≈ 7.09), the same rocket appears only 14 m long to an external observer.

subtopic.name: Length Contraction
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers proper length, contracted length, and the application of L = L₀/γ. It examines which observer measures the proper length and how contraction only occurs in the direction of relative motion.
subtopic.why: Length contraction is the spatial counterpart of time dilation. Together they ensure that all observers measure the same speed of light. Length contraction also has direct engineering consequences — particle accelerator drift tubes must be designed with it in mind.

items.title: I can explain why particle accelerator drift tubes must account for length contraction
items.what: In a linear accelerator (linac), charged particles travel through a series of drift tubes. The timing of the alternating voltage is set to match the time the particle spends inside each tube. Since particles travel at relativistic speeds, the drift tubes are contracted in the particle's reference frame — engineers must design tube lengths based on this contracted measurement.
items.why: If length contraction were ignored in the design, the alternating voltage would switch at the wrong moment, decelerating the particle rather than accelerating it. This is a direct, practical application of special relativity.
items.example: A proton at 0.995c (γ = 10) passes through a drift tube that is 85.5 cm long in the particle's frame. The proper length of the tube as measured in the lab is 85.5 × 10 = 855 mm = 85.5 cm × 10 = 85.5 cm × γ = 85.5 cm in the particle frame, so L₀ = 85.5 × 10 = 855 mm.

subtopic.name: Length Contraction
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers proper length, contracted length, and the application of L = L₀/γ. It examines which observer measures the proper length and how contraction only occurs in the direction of relative motion.
subtopic.why: Length contraction is the spatial counterpart of time dilation. Together they ensure that all observers measure the same speed of light. Length contraction also has direct engineering consequences — particle accelerator drift tubes must be designed with it in mind.

items.title: I can explain why classical physics predicts muons should not reach Earth's surface
items.what: Muons have a mean lifetime of 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ s when at rest. At 0.995c, classical physics predicts they travel only s = vt = 0.995 × 3.00 × 10⁸ × 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ ≈ 657 m before decaying. The upper atmosphere where muons are created is approximately 5000 m above the surface.
items.why: Establishing the classical prediction first gives a clear baseline for what special relativity must explain. It shows the genuine conflict between Newtonian mechanics and observation.
items.example: Using s = vt: s = 0.995 × 3.00 × 10⁸ × 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ = 657 m. Since 657 m is far less than 5000 m, classical physics predicts muons should decay well before reaching the ground.

subtopic.name: Muon Decay
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines muon decay as experimental evidence for special relativity. Muons created in the upper atmosphere at ~0.995c are detected at Earth's surface, which is impossible to explain using classical physics but is fully explained by either time dilation (from Earth's frame) or length contraction (from the muon's frame).
subtopic.why: Muon decay is one of the most important and accessible pieces of real-world evidence for special relativity. It demonstrates that the theory has genuine predictive power, and it requires students to reason carefully about which effect applies in which reference frame.

items.title: I can explain muon survival from Earth's reference frame using time dilation
items.what: From an observer on Earth, the muon is moving at 0.995c. The muon's lifetime is therefore dilated. The Earth observer measures the muon's lifetime as t = γt₀, which is much longer than 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ s, giving the muon enough time to travel 5000 m.
items.why: This is the standard Earth-frame explanation of muon survival. It directly applies the time dilation formula in a physically meaningful context.

subtopic.name: Muon Decay
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines muon decay as experimental evidence for special relativity. Muons created in the upper atmosphere at ~0.995c are detected at Earth's surface, which is impossible to explain using classical physics but is fully explained by either time dilation (from Earth's frame) or length contraction (from the muon's frame).
subtopic.why: Muon decay is one of the most important and accessible pieces of real-world evidence for special relativity. It demonstrates that the theory has genuine predictive power, and it requires students to reason carefully about which effect applies in which reference frame.

items.title: I can explain muon survival from the muon's reference frame using length contraction
items.what: In the muon's own reference frame, the muon is stationary and Earth is rushing toward it at 0.995c. The distance from the point of creation to Earth's surface is therefore length-contracted. The contracted distance is small enough for the muon to cover in its lifetime of 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ s.
items.why: This frame-of-reference explanation is equally valid and demonstrates that both time dilation and length contraction are different perspectives on the same physical outcome. VCE exam questions often specifically ask for the muon's frame explanation.
items.example: L = L₀ / γ = 5000 / 10.01 = 499 m. In its own frame, the muon only needs to 'travel' 499 m (Earth comes to it), which it easily covers in 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ s: d = 0.995 × 3.00 × 10⁸ × 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ = 657 m > 499 m.

Muons created in the upper atmosphere at ~0.995c are detected at Earth's surface, which is impossible to explain using classical physics but is fully explained by either time dilation (from Earth's frame) or length contraction (from the muon's frame).
subtopic.why: Muon decay is one of the most important and accessible pieces of real-world evidence for special relativity. It demonstrates that the theory has genuine predictive power, and it requires students to reason carefully about which effect applies in which reference frame.

items.title: I can identify which relativistic effect (time dilation or length contraction) is relevant based on the reference frame specified in a question
items.what: When a question asks for an explanation from Earth's frame, time dilation applies (the muon's lifetime is dilated as seen by Earth). When a question asks for an explanation from the muon's frame, length contraction applies (the distance to Earth is contracted as seen by the muon).
items.why: A common exam error is applying the wrong effect to the wrong frame. Both effects give consistent results but only one is logically valid for a given frame.
items.example: If the question says 'from the perspective of the muon', the answer must discuss length contraction of the distance to Earth, not time dilation of the muon's lifetime. Using time dilation in the muon's own frame would mean the muon ages more slowly relative to itself — which is meaningless.

Muons created in the upper atmosphere at ~0.995c are detected at Earth's surface, which is impossible to explain using classical physics but is fully explained by either time dilation (from Earth's frame) or length contraction (from the muon's frame).
subtopic.why: Muon decay is one of the most important and accessible pieces of real-world evidence for special relativity. It demonstrates that the theory has genuine predictive power, and it requires students to reason carefully about which effect applies in which reference frame.

items.title: I can apply E₀ = mc² to convert between rest mass and rest energy
items.what: The rest energy E₀ of an object is the energy equivalent of its mass when it is stationary. Even at rest, every object with mass has enormous energy stored within it, given by E₀ = mc².
items.why: This is the foundational formula of mass–energy equivalence and is used in all calculations involving mass conversion to energy, including nuclear fusion and annihilation.
items.example: An electron has a rest mass of 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. Its rest energy is E₀ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J = 0.511 MeV.

subtopic.name: Mass–Energy Equivalence
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Einstein's relationship between mass and energy: E₀ = mc², total relativistic energy Etot = γmc², and relativistic kinetic energy Ek = (γ − 1)mc². It applies these to nuclear fusion, positron–electron annihilation, and nuclear transmutation in particle accelerators.
subtopic.why: Mass–energy equivalence is one of the most profound results of special relativity. It explains how the Sun produces energy, how PET scans work, and how particle accelerators can create new particles. It also demonstrates that the classical kinetic energy formula ½mv² fails at high speeds.

items.title: I can calculate total relativistic energy using Etot = γmc²
items.what: The total energy of a moving object is Etot = γmc², where γ is the Lorentz factor. This includes both the rest energy E₀ = mc² and the relativistic kinetic energy. As v → c, Etot → ∞.
items.why: Total energy is conserved in all physical processes. This formula is needed for any calculation involving the energy of a relativistic particle, including those in particle accelerators.
items.example: A proton (m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) moving at 0.999c (γ = 22.4) has total energy Etot = 22.4 × 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 3.36 × 10⁻⁹ J.

subtopic.name: Mass–Energy Equivalence
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Einstein's relationship between mass and energy: E₀ = mc², total relativistic energy Etot = γmc², and relativistic kinetic energy Ek = (γ − 1)mc². It applies these to nuclear fusion, positron–electron annihilation, and nuclear transmutation in particle accelerators.
subtopic.why: Mass–energy equivalence is one of the most profound results of special relativity. It explains how the Sun produces energy, how PET scans work, and how particle accelerators can create new particles. It also demonstrates that the classical kinetic energy formula ½mv² fails at high speeds.

items.title: I can calculate relativistic kinetic energy using Ek = (γ − 1)mc²
items.what: Relativistic kinetic energy is the total energy minus the rest energy: Ek = (γ − 1)mc². At low speeds this approximates the classical ½mv², but at relativistic speeds it is significantly larger and approaches infinity as v approaches c.
items.why: The classical formula ½mv² fails for particles moving near the speed of light. Using it for particles in accelerators gives serious errors. The relativistic formula shows why particles cannot be accelerated to the speed of light — the energy required becomes infinite.

items.title: I can apply ΔE = Δmc² to calculate energy released in nuclear fusion
items.what: In nuclear fusion, lighter nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus. The products have slightly less mass than the reactants — this mass defect Δm is converted to energy according to ΔE = Δmc².
items.why: Nuclear fusion is the energy source of the Sun and stars. Understanding mass defect and energy release from E = Δmc² is a direct application of Einstein's formula to real physical processes.

It applies these to nuclear fusion, positron–electron annihilation, and nuclear transmutation in particle accelerators.

It explains how the Sun produces energy, how PET scans work, and how particle accelerators can create new particles. items.title: I can apply ΔE = Δmc² to calculate energy released in positron–electron annihilation
items.what: When a positron and electron meet, they annihilate completely, converting all of their combined rest mass into energy in the form of two gamma rays emitted in opposite directions. Each gamma ray carries energy equal to the rest energy of one electron.
items.why: Positron–electron annihilation is a direct and complete conversion of mass to energy. It is also the physical basis of PET scans used in medical imaging.
items.example: Each gamma ray has energy E = mc² = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J = 0.511 MeV. Total energy released = 2 × 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J.

It also demonstrates that the classical kinetic energy formula ½mv² fails at high speeds.

items.title: I can apply ΔE = Δmc² to nuclear transmutation in particle accelerators
items.what: When particles collide at high speed in an accelerator, nuclei can be broken apart and rearranged, producing different elements — this is nuclear transmutation. The mass difference between reactants and products is accounted for by the energy released or absorbed in the collision.
items.why: Particle accelerators are used to study nuclear structure and create new elements. The mass–energy relationship is what makes it possible to predict and quantify the energy involved in these collisions.
items.example: In a collision, reactants have combined mass 3.67 × 10⁻²⁵ kg and products have mass 3.60 × 10⁻²⁵ kg. Mass defect Δm = 0.07 × 10⁻²⁵ kg. Energy released: ΔE = 0.07 × 10⁻²⁵ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 6.30 × 10⁻¹⁰ J.

subtopic.name: Mass–Energy Equivalence
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Einstein's relationship between mass and energy: E₀ = mc², total relativistic energy Etot = γmc², and relativistic kinetic energy Ek = (γ − 1)mc². It applies these to nuclear fusion, positron–electron annihilation, and nuclear transmutation in particle accelerators.
subtopic.why: Mass–energy equivalence is one of the most profound results of special relativity. It explains how the Sun produces energy, how PET scans work, and how particle accelerators can create new particles. It also demonstrates that the classical kinetic energy formula ½mv² fails at high speeds.

items.title: I can interpret a graph of Lorentz factor (γ) vs relative speed and explain its implications for energy and mass
items.what: The Lorentz factor γ starts at 1 when v = 0 and increases gradually, then steeply, approaching infinity as v approaches c. This means total energy and kinetic energy both approach infinity as speed approaches c.
items.why: This graph shows visually why it is impossible to accelerate a massive object to the speed of light — infinite energy would be required. It also explains why relativistic effects are negligible at everyday speeds.
items.example: At v = 0.1c, γ ≈ 1.005 — barely any effect. At v = 0.9c, γ ≈ 2.29. At v = 0.99c, γ ≈ 7.09. At v = 0.999c, γ ≈ 22.4. The curve rises steeply near v = c.

items.title: I can explain why GPS satellite clocks must be corrected for time dilation
items.what: GPS satellites orbit at approximately 4 km/s. At this speed, special relativity predicts that their onboard clocks run slightly slower than clocks on Earth — by about 7 microseconds per day due to time dilation. Without correction, GPS position calculations would accumulate errors of approximately 10 km per day.
items.why: GPS is a direct, practical example of special relativity affecting everyday technology. It demonstrates that relativistic effects, though small at satellite speeds, are large enough to matter for precision engineering.
items.example: A GPS satellite clock runs slow by 7 μs per day due to its orbital speed. Position is calculated using s = cΔt, so a 7 μs error translates to a 7 × 10⁻⁶ × 3.00 × 10⁸ = 2100 m = 2.1 km error per day from time dilation alone.

subtopic.name: Applications of Relativity
subtopic.what: This subtopic pulls together the applications of special relativity to real-world systems: GPS satellite timing corrections, particle accelerator design, and the production of new elements through nuclear transmutation. It reinforces how relativity is not just theoretical but has direct engineering and technological consequences.
subtopic.why: Connecting the abstract mathematics of special relativity to GPS technology and particle physics helps students see that the theory has genuine, measurable consequences. These examples also frequently appear in VCE exam questions.

items.title: I can explain why particle accelerator drift tubes must be designed using length contraction
items.what: In a linear accelerator, particles travel through drift tubes at relativistic speeds. From the particle's reference frame, the drift tubes are length-contracted. The timing of the alternating voltage that accelerates the particle is based on how long the particle spends inside the tube — which depends on the contracted length in the particle's frame.
items.why: If engineers designed the drift tubes using only the lab-frame (proper) length, the voltage timing would be wrong and the particle would not be accelerated correctly. This is a concrete, testable engineering consequence of length contraction.
items.example: A proton at 0.995c (γ = 10.01) passes through a drift tube that engineers measure to be 85.5 cm in the lab. In the proton's frame, this tube appears contracted: L = 85.5 / 10.01 = 8.54 cm. The tube timing must be designed around 8.54 cm, not 85.5 cm.

items.title: I can explain how particle accelerators can produce new elements through nuclear transmutation
items.what: When particles are accelerated to relativistic speeds and collide, their kinetic energy can exceed the binding energy of nuclei. This allows nuclei to be broken apart and rearranged, changing the number of protons and neutrons — converting one element into another. This process is nuclear transmutation.
items.why: Nuclear transmutation in accelerators demonstrates that mass and energy are interconvertible and that the periodic table is not fixed — elements can be created and destroyed. It also shows why charged particles must be used: they can be accelerated by electric fields.
items.example: At the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, carbon and neon beams were accelerated and fired into bismuth foil. The collisions changed the atomic number of some bismuth nuclei, producing radioactive gold isotopes — fulfilling the ancient alchemist dream by modern physics.
